733dc4d8dc.q: What did Andrew Scott learn about employee engagement from six years at Goldman Sachs managing benefits for 30,000 employees?
733dc4d8dc.a: Scott discovered that even world-class benefits fail to drive health improvements if they don't fit into employees' real lives. At Goldman Sachs, despite offering top-notch benefits, engagement remained challenging because highly intelligent and busy employees lacked time to navigate the complex healthcare system. He learned that people engage with benefits only when they become relevant at the exact moment they need them, not based on awareness alone.

0744eb1048.q: Why do employers struggle with healthcare vendor proliferation when they could optimize existing solutions?
0744eb1048.a: Most employers don't have a benefits problem but rather a fragmentation problem where solutions live in silos without integrating or communicating. Andrew Scott argues that more resources and services don't necessarily create more opportunity; instead, more choice can create friction. The real issue is not acquiring new solutions but achieving value realization from current offerings and addressing fragmentation.

ea800a34ef.q: What does Andrew Scott recommend benefits leaders ask prospective healthcare vendors about their role in the employee journey?
ea800a34ef.a: Scott advises asking vendors 'Show me where you fit in this member journey' and what they do when a member needs something outside their scope. He emphasizes that great healthcare partners shouldn't try to own every member or offer everything. Instead, they should know when to hand off members to more appropriate services and demonstrate this through referral data, showing they recognize when employees need additional support like EAP benefits.

9fa8eb856e.q: How can data analytics identify employees who may be suffering in silence from health issues they don't realize they can address?
9fa8eb856e.a: Scott explains that technology now enables identification of leading indicators suggesting an employee may be struggling. For example, if data shows an employee visited a chiropractor three times in four weeks, this suggests musculoskeletal pain, yet they may not be using their free physical therapy benefit. Targeted interventions can then alert them to available resources rather than sending generic awareness messaging that gets lost.

de611378d3.q: What is the 'paradox of choice' problem in employee benefits design, and how does it parallel streaming service fragmentation?
de611378d3.a: Scott describes how too many benefit options create decision paralysis and reduce engagement, similar to how multiple streaming services complicate content discovery. Just as a hypothetical Roku or Google plugin could aggregate streaming services and identify cost overlaps, employers need a platform that consolidates all their disparate benefits, shows employees where services overlap, and reveals when they're overpaying for duplicate coverage, allowing better decision-making and cost optimization.
